sections.title: The Prohibition of Cooking Meat and Milk
sections.html:
The Torah forbade cooking meat with milk, as it is stated: "You shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk." This prohibition is mentioned three times in the Torah (Shemot 23:19; 34:26; Devarim 14:21), to teach us that the prohibition has three parts: 1) It is forbidden to cook them together. 2) If they were cooked together, it is forbidden to eat them. 3) If they were cooked together, it is also forbidden to derive benefit from them (Ḥullin 115b; SA YD 87:1).

This prohibition is unique and different from the other prohibitions of eating, for all the forbidden foods are always forbidden, whereas meat on its own is kosher and milk on its own is kosher, and cooking them together is forbidden, and if they were cooked together – they become forbidden with an especially severe prohibition. For all the other forbidden foods, such as the meat of impure domesticated and wild animals, a Jew is permitted to cook for a non-Jew, but meat and milk a Jew is forbidden to cook for a non-Jew. It is even forbidden to assist in cooking them, for example by raising the flame on which they are cooking. In addition, meat and milk that were cooked together are forbidden for benefit, and therefore it is forbidden to sell them to a non-Jew, and it is even forbidden to give them to him as a gift, since the Jew derives benefit from this. And even if one burns them, it is forbidden to benefit from the heat of their burning or from the ash that results from them. It is even forbidden to place them before ownerless animals, since the Jew derives satisfaction from this. Rather, one must bury the forbidden food, and when it is difficult to bury it, one may throw it into a field or into the garbage bin. And although it is likely that animals will eat from it, there is no prohibition in this, since he does not intend this.1

By Torah law the prohibition is to cook meat with milk, and without cooking there is no prohibition. Therefore, it is permitted to mix them together without cooking for the needs of a non-Jew or for any other need. The Sages made a fence around the Torah and forbade a Jew to eat meat and milk together even without cooking (SA YD 87:1; 91:8), and the Sages reinforced this fence with many prohibitions: they forbade eating one kind when the other kind is placed on the table (below, halakha 3), and they forbade baking meat or dairy bread lest it be eaten with the other kind (below, halakha 4). They even went further and forbade eating milk after meat without a significant wait, and forbade eating meat after milk without cleaning the mouth (as explained in the next chapter). The reason for all these decrees is explained below (halakha 5).

sections.title: The Meat and Milk Included in the Prohibition
sections.html:
The Tanna'im disagreed about which kinds of meat and milk are included in the Torah prohibition. According to Rabbi Akiva, the meat and milk that were forbidden are those of one of the three species of pure domesticated animals (behema): cattle, sheep and goats. However, the seven species of pure wild animals (ḥaya), such as the deer and the ayal, are not included in the Torah prohibition. This law too we learned from the fact that the Torah repeated the prohibition "You shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk" three times, to teach us that the three species of pure domesticated animals are included in the prohibition, whereas the species of pure wild animals, pure birds, and impure domesticated and wild animals are not included in the prohibition (Mishna Ḥullin 113a). The difference between domesticated and wild animals is that domesticated animals are tame and wild animals are not tame. Since domesticated animals are in a person's possession, he can milk them and slaughter their offspring, and the Torah forbade mixing the meat of one of the domesticated animals with the milk of one of the domesticated animals. The Torah gave the example of a young goat in its mother's milk, because the goat's milk is plentiful, and it often gives birth to two kids, and after the kids had grown a little, people would slaughter one in order to eat its meat, and since its mother continued to nurse the second kid, it was common for them to cook the kid's meat in its mother's milk (Rashbam, Shemot 23:19).

According to Rabbi Yossi Ha-gelili, the seven species of pure wild animals are also included in the Torah prohibition, since they too have meat and milk that are permitted to be eaten, but fowl is not included in the prohibition, since the female bird has no milk. And some say that fowl meat is also included in the Torah prohibition, since it too is a kind of meat. The proof is that it must be slaughtered in order to permit its meat.

In practice, the halakha was ruled according to Rabbi Akiva, that the Torah prohibition applies only to species of domesticated animals, and by rabbinic law it is forbidden to eat wild animals and fowl with milk as well, but it is permitted to cook them for a non-Jew and permitted to derive benefit from them (SA YD 87:2).2

sections.title: Eating at One Table
sections.html:
The Sages enacted that when a person eats a meat food, no dairy food should be placed on his table, and when he eats a dairy food, no meat food should be placed on his table, so that he will not mistakenly eat them together. And not only the meat of domesticated animals is included in the prohibition, but also the meat of fowl and wild animals (Ḥullin 103b; 104b; SA 88:1). But one who has eaten meat is permitted to prepare dairy foods before six hours have passed for him. For the enactment was intended to serve as a fence against eating the two kinds together, and not to safeguard the waiting period between eating meat and eating milk (see Arukh Ha-shulḥan 11 and Darkhei Teshuva 16).

The Sages also enacted that two people who know each other should not eat at one table, this one meat and that one milk, lest one come to eat from his fellow's food and thus be found eating meat with milk. But they did not forbid two strangers who happened to come to one place to eat at one table, this one meat and that one milk, because a stranger is not accustomed to take food from his neighbour (Ḥullin 107b). If the two people who know each other place a sign between them that will remind them to keep apart from each other's food, they may eat together at one table. As a sign, one may place a utensil or food that is not usually placed there, and likewise one may spread a separate tablecloth for one of them (SA 88:2). And if they sit far from each other, so that neither can stretch out his hand and reach his fellow's food, they are permitted to eat at one table without a sign (Yam Shel Shlomo and Baḥ). One who has finished eating meat may sit next to his fellow who is eating milk and eat pareve foods, even though six hours have not yet passed for him.3

sections.title: Baking Dairy or Meat Bread
sections.html:
The Sages decreed that one should not knead bread dough with milk, lest people forget that the bread is dairy and come to eat it with meat. Likewise they decreed that one should not knead it with meat fat, lest people forget that the bread is meaty and come to eat it with milk. If one erred and kneaded bread dough with milk or with meat fat, the Sages decreed that the bread is forbidden to be eaten (Pesaḥim 30a-b).

The prohibition is to prepare bread that is eaten over the course of more than one meal, but it is permitted to prepare dairy or meat bread in a quantity that the household will finish at the next meal, since there is no concern that by the next meal they will forget that it is dairy or meaty.

Likewise it is permitted to prepare dairy or meat bread when one changes the bread's shape, in such a way that the household will understand that its status is different and will find out whether it is dairy or meaty. But such a sign does not permit baking dairy or meat bread in order to sell it, lest there be people who will not notice the sign. Only when one makes a clear sign from which everyone understands that this bread is dairy or meaty is it permitted, such as a pita with yellow cheese or a strip of meat stuck on it (Pesaḥim 36a; SA 97:1).

The prohibition applies specifically to bread, which people are accustomed to eat with dairy or meat foods. The same applies to crackers, which are sometimes eaten with cheese and sometimes with sausage. But cakes and other baked goods may be prepared dairy or meaty, since they are generally not eaten with meat or milk (Maharit 2, YD 18).4

sections.title: The Reason for the Additional Decrees Concerning Meat and Milk
sections.html:
It is fitting to ask: is it not a well-known rule that the Sages do not enact a decree upon a decree, whereas in the prohibition of eating meat at a table on which there is milk, and likewise in the prohibition of baking dairy or meat bread, they enacted a decree upon a decree? For only meat and milk that were cooked together are forbidden to be eaten by Torah law, and the Sages decreed that one may not eat meat with milk even if they were not cooked together; why then did they go further and decree a decree upon a decree, forbidding even bringing meat and milk together onto the table during the meal, and likewise forbidding baking dairy or meat bread?

The commentators explained that with regard to the prohibition of meat and milk the concern of a mishap is especially great, since meat on its own is permitted and milk on its own is permitted, and both are found in the kitchen, and they can easily become mixed, and therefore it was necessary to enact decrees upon decrees concerning them. Furthermore, had the Sages not added decrees in this matter, even the basic decrees would not have been observed; therefore all the decrees are considered one decree intended to fortify the separation between meat and milk.

Not only that, but in all the decrees concerning eating, they equated the meat of fowl and wild animals, whose prohibition is rabbinic, with the meat of domesticated animals, whose prohibition is from the Torah, because if people were lenient with fowl or wild animals, they would mistakenly be lenient with the meat of domesticated animals as well.5

sections.title: Separation Between Meat and Dairy Foods
sections.html:
One who wishes to eat meat at a table on which milk was eaten, or vice versa, must clean the table of the remnants of the previous food, and without this it is forbidden to eat the other kind at that table. Likewise it is forbidden to eat meat on a tablecloth on which dairy foods were eaten, or vice versa, unless it is clean of the remnants of the previous food (SA 89:4). If the tablecloth is made of fabric that absorbs dirt, it must be laundered. And if it is made of plastic that does not absorb dirt, one may clean it with a damp cloth. Even when one is careful to place the foods inside plates, one must clean the table between eating meat and milk.

Bread that was served at a meat meal, if there is a reasonable concern that people touched it with hands that had fat or meat gravy on them, should not be served at a dairy meal, so that people will not come to eat remnants of meat with milk, and likewise the reverse (SA 89:4). And if people were careful not to touch the bread with hands to which fat or gravy was stuck, it is permitted to eat it at a dairy meal (see SA 91:3).

Salads that were served at a meat meal, if there is a reasonable concern that the diners took from them with cutlery that had meat remnants on it, should not be served at a dairy meal, and likewise the reverse. And if the salads have their own serving spoons, and there is no concern that one of the diners took from them with cutlery bearing meat remnants, it is permitted to serve them at a dairy meal, and likewise the reverse. Some are stringent le-khatḥila (from the outset), that no foods served at a meat meal should be served at a dairy meal, and likewise the reverse. And even those who are meticulous about this may be lenient when necessary, as long as there is no reasonable concern that remnants of milk or meat stuck to the salad or the bread.6

As we learned (in halakha 3), while eating meat it is forbidden for milk to be on the table, and likewise the reverse, lest people mistakenly eat them together. But not at the time of eating, it is permitted to place them on one table (Ḥullin 104b; SA 88:1). Likewise it is permitted to place pieces of meat and cheese in one bag, or in one drawer in a cupboard or in the refrigerator, while taking care that they do not touch each other. And if they touched each other, one rinses the place where they touched and it is permitted to eat them (Ḥullin 107b; SA 91:1-2; below 35:1).

Similarly, one should not place milk bags in a place from which they may drip onto meat foods, and if it dripped, one must rinse the meat until not a trace of the milk's taste remains in it, and then it is permitted to eat it and cook it.7

sections.title: Separation Between the Utensils
sections.html:
In a kitchen where dairy and meat foods are prepared, one must designate separate cooking utensils for milk and separate cooking utensils for meat, and it is proper that there be a noticeable difference between them, so that they will not be mistakenly interchanged. Likewise one must designate a set of plates and cutlery for dairy foods and a set of plates and cutlery for meat foods, and it is proper that there be a noticeable difference between them, so that they will not be interchanged. It is also proper to assign each kind a special place so that they will not become mixed. Even when eating cold meat or dairy foods, the custom of Israel is to maintain the separation between the utensils, and to eat and serve dairy foods in dairy utensils and meat foods in meat utensils, in order to prevent mishaps and mixing between them.

Many are accustomed to designate two salt shakers, one for dairy meals and one for meat meals. For sometimes the salt shaker touches the foods, and sometimes people touch the salt shaker with hands that have gravy on them, and if one salt shaker is used for both kinds, there is a concern that through it a trace of taste of one kind will become mixed into the other. And if one wishes to use one salt shaker for meat and dairy, one must take care that it be clean, and if it became soiled with a trace of food, wipe it well.

Those who use bottles containing sauces or ketchup for both dairy and meat meals must take care that the nozzle does not touch the foods, so that nothing from the dairy or meat foods will stick to it. Likewise they must take care not to touch these containers with hands to which a trace of moisture from meat or dairy foods is stuck. And if they were not careful about this, one must wipe the container and its nozzle, so that a trace of taste of one kind will not reach the other through them.

The tray of a baby's high chair: since generally one does not place on it food that is yad soledet bo (hot enough that the hand recoils from it), so as not to harm the baby, there is no concern that the tray will absorb the taste of meat or milk, and all that is necessary is to clean the tray well between meals. However, one who sometimes places on the tray food that is yad soledet bo must determine that the tray will be meat or dairy, and if he wishes to place on it something of the other kind, he should clean the tray beforehand and take care that the food of the other kind does not reach the heat of yad soledet bo.

sections.title: Pareve Foods
sections.html:
A pareve food is a food that is neither dairy nor meaty. Le-khatḥila one should maintain the separation between the kinds, and when one intends to eat pareve foods with meat – cook them in a meat pot; and when one intends to eat them with milk – cook them in a dairy pot. This is in order to prevent confusion, for if people become accustomed to eating with milk pareve foods that were cooked in a meat pot, it is possible that they will sometimes err and think that a meat food is pareve and come to eat it with milk, or the reverse. There is also a concern that sometimes the utensils will not be cleaned well, and then there is a remote concern that the pareve food will absorb taste from the pot and become meaty or dairy, and people will mistakenly eat it with the other kind.

However, when necessary, it is permitted to cook a pareve food in a clean meat pot of metal or glass in order to eat it afterwards with milk, or the reverse. Likewise, when necessary, it is permitted to cut sharp foods such as onion and garlic with a meat metal knife that was cleaned well, for a dairy dish, or the reverse. Admittedly, some are stringent and forbid eating with milk a pareve food that was cooked in a meat utensil, or the reverse. However, since it is clear beyond any doubt that after glass and metal utensils are cleaned with soap they do not emit tastes (below 32:6; 8), the halakha follows the lenient opinion (below 32:11-12).

But if the pareve food was cooked in a meat or dairy metal or glass pot that was not cleaned well with soap, the poskim disagree as to whether it is permitted to eat the pareve dish with the other kind. Likewise, if the pareve food was cooked in a meat or dairy earthenware utensil, even though it was cleaned well with soap, since earthenware absorbs tastes into itself, the poskim disagree as to whether it is permitted to eat it with the other kind. 8

A wooden or plastic cutting board absorbs tastes; therefore one should designate a special board for meat foods and a special board for dairy foods. And one who wishes to cut foods for both kinds should also designate a board for pareve food. Be-di'avad (after the fact), if vegetables were cut on a meat cutting board that was cleaned well, and they were mixed into a dairy dish, the dish is kosher. But if the vegetables were sharp, such as onion, and the dish did not contain sixty times the onion, the dish should be forbidden to be eaten, lest a taste of milk [?] entered it through the onion. In a pressing situation one may be lenient (below 32:12).

sections.title: Mixing Utensils
sections.html:
Even when one wishes to prepare a cold pareve food, it is proper to prepare it with a set of utensils of one kind, dairy or meat, in order to maintain the separation between meat and dairy utensils. For example, when preparing the pareve food in a meat bowl, it is proper to stir it with a meat spoon. However, when necessary, for example when one is in a hurry and there is no washed meat spoon there, one may stir the pareve food with a dairy spoon, or the reverse.9

In kitchens with many workers, such as the kitchens of educational institutions, experience has shown that without setting strict procedures, the concern of confusion between meat and milk increases. All the more so when some of the workers are not meticulous in observing mitzvot, as in army kitchens and in the kitchens of event halls, hotels and restaurants. Therefore it is customary to set for public kitchens separation procedures that are much stricter than what is customary in home kitchens, and this is entrusted to the rabbis responsible for granting kashrut certificates, who, according to their experience and their acquaintance with the kitchen workers, set the separation procedures needed to maintain kashrut.

sections.title: Pareve Utensils
sections.html:
By law there is no need to keep pareve utensils, for even when one wishes to cook a pareve food and eat part of it with meat and part of it with milk, one may cook it in a clean meat or dairy metal pot (as explained in halakha 8). However, in practice, many are accustomed to be meticulous and keep pareve utensils, in order to prepare in them foods part of which they wish to eat with meat and part with milk. One of the reasons for this meticulousness is the concern that sometimes the utensils are not cleaned well and a taste of meat or milk remains in them. This meticulousness has become more widespread as the prices of utensils have fallen.

On the other hand, some prefer from the outset not to keep pareve utensils, because confusion sometimes arises from them, for people are accustomed to be careful about the separation between meat and milk, but they are not accustomed to be so careful about pareve, and perhaps they will mistakenly cook a meat dish in a pareve pot and afterwards mistakenly mix it with milk, or the reverse. Also, people do not know whether to wash the pareve utensils with the meat utensils or with the dairy ones.

For those who are accustomed to use pareve utensils, if they erred and cooked a meat or dairy food in a pareve utensil, they kasher the utensil by hagala (koshering in boiling water) in order to restore it to pareve status. If boiling milk or boiling meat gravy spilled on it, one wipes off the gravy and pours boiling water on that spot, in order to keep it pareve.

By law it is permitted to wash pareve utensils in a dishwasher or in a sink together with meat or dairy utensils, and they remain pareve. However, when dealing with a poor dishwasher in which remnants of fats and foods remain, one should not wash pareve utensils in it together with meat or dairy utensils. Likewise in a sink, if the utensils are soaked there with very hot water, or for twenty-four hours or more, one should not soak pareve utensils with dairy or meat utensils. Indeed, this is one of the confusions that may arise from pareve utensils, that the clear separation between meat and milk becomes blurred, and therefore some are meticulous to always wash the pareve utensils separately.

sections.title: Mistakes and Mishaps
sections.html:
When cooking a pareve dish in a meat pot, one should not stir it with a dairy spoon, and likewise the reverse. If one erred and stirred, as long as the pot and the spoon were made of metal, and were clean before the cooking began, the dish is kosher and the spoon does not need koshering.

If one erred and stirred a meat dish with a dairy metal spoon, or the reverse: if the spoon was clean, be-di'avad the dish is kosher, since a clean metal spoon does not emit tastes. But the spoon needs koshering by hagala, because it was used once in boiling milk and once in boiling meat (below 32, note 11).

Sometimes one cooks on the stovetop at the same time a meat dish and a dairy or pareve dish in a dairy metal pot, and if gravy from the meat pot splashed onto the walls of the dairy pot, since the whole pot was boiling hot, the whole pot needs koshering by hagala. However, the dish inside it is kosher, since the taste does not pass to it from the splash through the metal.10

If boiling meat gravy splashed onto the wall of a cold dairy metal pot, or the reverse, since the pot that received the splash was cold, only its outer layer was affected by the splash, and therefore there is no need to kasher all of it by hagala; rather it suffices to pour boiling water from a kettle on the spot where the gravy splashed, in accordance with the rule "ke-bol'o kakh polto" (as it absorbed, so it expels). This is how it is done: one wipes the gravy off the pot and pours boiling water on that spot. It is customary to pour water there abundantly, in a quantity sixty times greater than the outer layer of the pot at the spot where the gravy splashed, and when there is doubt whether the water is sixty times the outer layer of the pot at that spot, one mixes soapy water into the water (Peninei Halakha, Pesaḥ 10:10; below 33:4).

If one erred and cut boiling hot meat with a dairy metal knife, if the knife was clean in the usual manner, the meat is kosher, and the knife needs koshering by hagala (below 32:8). And if the meat was cold, the knife needs a good cleaning but does not need koshering.

sections.title: The Custom of Two Sinks and the Law of Dishwashers
sections.html:
It is customary to install two sinks, one for washing dairy utensils and one for washing meat utensils. Likewise it is customary to designate one side of the counter for dairy foods and the other side for meat foods. Pareve foods may be prepared on both parts of the counter, provided that the counter is clean. When necessary, one may use one sink and one counter for both kinds, provided that one takes care to clean the sink and the counter of food remnants between one kind and the other.11

It is customary to designate separate scrubbing cloths for dairy and for meat. However, by law, as long as soap is mixed with the water, it is permitted to scrub meat and dairy utensils with the same cloth, for the soap spoils the tastes of the foods in such a way that they are no longer considered meaty or dairy.

Dishwasher: It is permitted to use the same dishwasher and the same racks for meat and dairy one after the other, while taking care not to wash them together, lest the tastes of meat and milk become mixed together before they are spoiled by the soap.

Some are accustomed to be meticulous and buy two racks, one for meat utensils and one for dairy utensils, in order to maintain the customary separation between meat utensils and dairy utensils, and some are meticulous to designate the dishwasher for one kind, and for the two kinds they install two dishwashers. However, as stated, according to the law, it is permitted to wash in the same dishwasher and on the same rack, once meat utensils and once dairy ones.12

sections.title: Stovetops
sections.html:
It is permitted to use the same grate for meat and for milk, because even if a little meat or dairy gravy boiled over onto the grate, the fire that prevails there burns and spoils what spilled. The same law applies to electric and ceramic stovetops: it is permitted to place on the same surface once a meat pot and once a dairy pot, since the heat of the stovetop burns what sometimes spills from them.13

When cooking on the stovetop at the same time a meat pot and a dairy pot, one should take care that space remains between them, so that one dish will not boil over onto the wall of the other pot. And if the two pots touched each other during the cooking, as long as there was no moisture connecting them at the place of contact, the pots and the dishes are kosher, for tastes do not pass through dry utensils (Rema 92:8). And if there was moisture connecting them, for example because one dish boiled over, the dishes are kosher and the pots need hagala (as explained in halakha 11).

One should be stringent not to eat foods that fell onto the metal surface beneath the grate, because sometimes there are remnants of meat and dairy foods there. And if a thick piece fell there, one may cut off and throw away a thickness of about two centimetres from the side that touched the surface and eat the rest. And if it is known that the surface was cleaned well and is still clean, it is permitted to eat what fell on it, since the whole concern is about the grease on it, but there is no need to be concerned that the surface absorbed taste that it will later emit. Likewise, if a dairy food fell there, and it is known that since the last cleaning no meat food was cooked there, the dairy food that fell there is kosher (below 32:8-9).

sections.title: Baking Ovens
sections.html:
The custom of Israel is to fortify the separation between meat and milk, and accordingly many are accustomed to buy an oven with two compartments, and to designate one for meat and one for dairy, or to buy an oven with one compartment and designate it for one of the kinds only. One who wishes to use the same compartment once for meat and once for dairy may do so, provided that he has a special baking tray for meat and a special baking tray for dairy, and he takes care to kasher it when switching between the two kinds by heating the oven for about half an hour at the highest temperature, and it is also customary to clean it beforehand. And even those who are meticulous not to use the same oven compartment once for meat and once for dairy may do so when necessary.14

Many are accustomed that when they wish to bake in a meat or dairy oven a pareve food that will be permitted to be eaten with both kinds – they first heat the oven at the highest temperature for about half an hour, in order to make it pareve. Those who wish to be lenient may bake the pareve food without koshering, for it is clear that there is no possibility at all that a taste of meat or milk will be sensed in the pareve food.

If one erred and cooked a dairy dish in a meat oven, be-di'avad the dairy dish is kosher, for in practice no real taste of meat entered the milk, and at most, if meat remnants remained in the oven, it is possible that vapours will rise that might give an odour of meat to the dairy dish, and be-di'avad odour does not render forbidden (see below 35:10). And the oven needs koshering by heating at the high temperature for half an hour.15

sections.title: Microwave Ovens
sections.html:
One may use the same microwave for dairy and meat foods while creating a separation between them. In the separation one must pay attention to two things: first, that dairy or meat foods not be placed directly on the same plate; second, that a large amount of condensation not enter the food being heated from the cavity of the microwave.

Therefore, one must take care not to place foods directly on the fixed plate of the microwave; rather, dairy foods should be placed on a dairy plate and meat foods on a meat plate, and these plates should be placed on the plate of the microwave. Likewise, one should designate a special cover for dairy foods and a special cover for meat foods. And although vapours come out through the small holes in covers intended for the microwave, the condensation that comes out of them does not have the power to accumulate on the walls and ceiling of the microwave and impart taste to it, and all the more so they do not have the power to draw out taste that may have been absorbed in the walls of the microwave and put it into the food being heated.

Alternatively, one may determine that the normal status of the microwave is dairy, and if one wishes to heat a meat food in it, one places another plate or another surface on the fixed plate of the microwave, and covers the meat foods with a cover or a box, or wraps them in a bag. One should do the same when heating a pareve food in order to eat it with meat foods.

A microwave that was used for non-kosher food must be koshered (below 33:9). Be-di'avad, when there is no time to kasher it, or when it belongs to people who are not careful about kashrut, one may heat foods in it by placing them on an additional plate and putting them inside a bag or box that will wrap them on all sides, even though an opening will remain there for vapours to escape.16
